power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
# table data --------------------------------------

"p < 0.05", "p < 0.05"), Text = c("With 4 h or 8 h bands, night departures and landings were 60 to 101 min below the evening (p ≤ 0.013).", 
"The morning departure contrast held with 4 h bands and the 24 h cycle but not with 8 h bands, and the morning landing contrast reached p < 0.05 under no definition.", 
"Shifting the 6 h bands 3 h later moved the evening reference past midnight, and no contrast then reached p < 0.05.", 
"For landings, only cut-offs at 10:00h and 11:00h reached p < 0.05 (-48 and -40 min; Supplementary Table S6).", 
"Without deadhead sectors, Equation (2) and its timezone-shift form still gave no direction or haul contrast with p < 0.05."
)), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------

```

text.text: Aviation fatigue management estimates crew sleep from rosters and self-report.
We examined how sleep duration changes around flights and with departure and landing times.
In an observational cohort study, 13 cargo pilots wore an Ultrahuman smart ring for six months in 2026.
We linked 1,504 sleep sessions to the flown schedule.
Linear mixed-effects models compared each sleep session with the same pilot's rest nights, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
Total sleep time was 48 min shorter on the night before a flight (95% CI 32 to 65 min) and 28 min shorter in the first sleep after one (95% CI 13 to 43 min).
Later nights did not differ.
Sleep duration varied with clock time.

Compared with evening departures and landings, respectively, pilots slept 57 min less before a departure between 06:00h and 11:59h (95% CI 14 to 101 min) and 97 min less after a landing between 00:00h and 05:59h (95% CI 37 to 156 min).
Flight direction and length showed no association.
Differences between pilots explained 14.1% of the variance in total sleep time, more than six times the 2.2% explained by duty position.
Fatigue risk management could plan rest around departure and landing times.
Fatigue is a recognized hazard in aviation, driven by long duty periods, circadian disruption and insufficient sleep (Caldwell et al. 2009).
text.formatted: Fatigue is a recognized hazard in aviation, driven by long duty periods, circadian disruption and insufficient sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Caldwell et al. 2009</ref>).

text.text: Regulators manage it with prescriptive duty limits (European Aviation Safety Agency 2014) and with fatigue risk management systems that monitor risk from operational data (International Civil Aviation Organization 2016; IATA et al. 2015; Federal Aviation Administration 2013).
text.formatted: Regulators manage it with prescriptive duty limits (European Aviation Safety Agency 2014) and with fatigue risk management systems that monitor risk from operational data <ref type="bibr">(International Civil Aviation Organization 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">IATA et al. 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Federal Aviation Administration 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Prescriptive limits scale duty with its length, its start time and the time zones it crosses (European Aviation Safety Agency 2014; Federal Aviation Administration 2012).
They bound duty and rest periods, not the sleep a pilot takes within them.
Biomathematical models predict fatigue from the roster, some by first inferring the sleep it allows (Hursh et al. 2004; Roach et al. 2004; Åkerstedt et al. 2004; Mallis et al. 2004).
text.formatted: Biomathematical models predict fatigue from the roster, some by first inferring the sleep it allows <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hursh et al. 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Roach et al. 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Åkerstedt et al. 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Mallis et al. 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Built from laboratory studies, they predict average fatigue without variation between individuals (Dawson et al. 2011).
text.formatted: Built from laboratory studies, they predict average fatigue without variation between individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Dawson et al. 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Neither route measures how much a given pilot sleeps on each night of a roster.
Field studies with actigraphy and sleep diaries, mostly in short-haul passenger flying, report shorter sleep around early starts and night duties.

Early starts were associated with about an hour less sleep before duty (Roach et al. 2012; Vejvoda et al. 2014), and night duty with shorter sleep in both short-and long-haul flying (Flynn-Evans et al. 2026; Sallinen et al. 2017).
text.formatted: Early starts were associated with about an hour less sleep before duty <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Roach et al. 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Vejvoda et al. 2014)</ref>, and night duty with shorter sleep in both short-and long-haul flying <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Flynn-Evans et al. 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Sallinen et al. 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These studies followed pilots for a few duty periods to about two months and compared one kind of duty with another.
Sleep, however, differs widely between people.
The differences are often as large as experimental effects, and sleep duration is trait-like (Van Dongen et al. 2005).
text.formatted: The differences are often as large as experimental effects, and sleep duration is trait-like <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Van Dongen et al. 2005)</ref>.

text.text: A duty night is therefore best judged against the same pilot's usual sleep, measured over many rest nights, which takes long-term tracking to establish a reliable baseline for each pilot.
How sleep loss spreads across a roster against that baseline is unclear.
Overnight cargo flying carries fatigue risks that daytime flying does not, yet the newest United States duty rule does not apply to all-cargo operations.
That 2012 rule limits duty by time of day and requires an 8 h sleep opportunity before each duty, so that passenger crews do not accumulate dangerous fatigue (Federal Aviation Administration 2012).
text.formatted: That 2012 rule limits duty by time of day and requires an 8 h sleep opportunity before each duty, so that passenger crews do not accumulate dangerous fatigue <ref type="bibr">(Federal Aviation Administration 2012)</ref>.

text.text: A flight-crew fatigue program at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration studied four types of air transport.
In two of them, overnight cargo and long-haul, crews sometimes flew at the circadian low point in alertness (Gander et al. 1998c).
text.formatted: In two of them, overnight cargo and long-haul, crews sometimes flew at the circadian low point in alertness <ref type="bibr">(Gander et al. 1998c)</ref>.

text.text: In its overnight cargo crews, daytime sleep was 41% shorter than night sleep, and the circadian rhythm did not fully adapt (Gander et al. 1998a).
text.formatted: In its overnight cargo crews, daytime sleep was 41% shorter than night sleep, and the circadian rhythm did not fully adapt <ref type="bibr">(Gander et al. 1998a)</ref>.

text.text: Those crews slept 1.2 h less per 24 h on duty days than before the trip (Gander et al. 1998a).
text.formatted: Those crews slept 1.2 h less per 24 h on duty days than before the trip <ref type="bibr">(Gander et al. 1998a)</ref>.

text.text: Field evidence on sleep in cargo operations remains thin.
Published cargo studies followed crews through single 8-day trips (Gander et al. 1998a) or five humanitarian missions used to test a biomathematical model (Devine et al. 2022).
text.formatted: Published cargo studies followed crews through single 8-day trips <ref type="bibr">(Gander et al. 1998a)</ref> or five humanitarian missions used to test a biomathematical model <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Devine et al. 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In comments on the 2012 rule, the cargo industry set its flying apart from passenger operations (Federal Aviation Administration 2012).
text.formatted: In comments on the 2012 rule, the cargo industry set its flying apart from passenger operations <ref type="bibr">(Federal Aviation Administration 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In its account, night flying and routings around the world in all directions, rather than quick turns at foreign destinations, are the norm.
One carrier's rotations can range from short turns to multi-week trips away from base, and most nights in a pilot's month are not flown.
Sleep loss measured over short windows of passenger flying may therefore not transfer to cargo schedules.
Single trips or missions were too short to show where in a roster sleep loss falls, or whether it persists between duties.

Here we tracked 13 cargo pilots long-term with a consumer smart ring, which records sleep timing and duration each night with adequate accuracy (Chinoy et al. 2021; de Zambotti et al. 2019; Svensson et al. 2024; Driller et al. 2026).
text.formatted: Here we tracked 13 cargo pilots long-term with a consumer smart ring, which records sleep timing and duration each night with adequate accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Chinoy et al. 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">de Zambotti et al. 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Svensson et al. 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Driller et al. 2026)</ref>.

text.text: We defined long-term tracking as six months of rostered duty.
We compared each night with the same pilot's rest nights, with total sleep time as the primary outcome.
We examined how total sleep time changed before and after flights, and how far the change extended.
We tested whether the clock times of departure and landing are associated with sleep duration immediately before and after flights, as early starts are in passenger flying.
We also tested whether the direction and length of the flight matter within one network.
Finally, we asked how much usual sleep differed between pilots, how sleep differences between home and away nights depend on trip pattern, and whether departure delays affect crew rest.
This was an observational cohort study (Figure 1a).
text.formatted: This was an observational cohort study (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1a</ref>).

text.text: We linked six months of longitudinal smart-ring sleep records from 13 pilots of one cargo carrier to the carrier's flown and planned schedules.
Each night was classified by its position relative to the pilot's flights and compared with the same pilot's rest nights.
Table 1 defines the terms used throughout, and Supplementary Figure S1 shows how each analysis sample was formed.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">1</ref> defines the terms used throughout, and Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S1</ref> shows how each analysis sample was formed.

text.text: We studied pilots of a cargo carrier that flies a long-haul freighter network and short-haul regional services from a single hub.
The carrier's trial crew list named 14 pilots.
Thirteen supplied ring data and formed the cohort; the fourteenth supplied none.
Pilots were enrolled in November 2025 to span the carrier's schedules, from short turns to multi-week rotations.
The cohort size was set by enrollment, and no sample-size calculation was made.
All 13 pilots were male, and the crew list recorded their rank but not their age or flying experience.
Sleep and schedule data were collected during routine duty from 1 January to 30 June 2026.
All pilots gave informed consent for the use of their wearable and operational data under the carrier's data-use agreement.
The study followed the Declaration of Helsinki.
The retrospective analysis was approved by the Medstar Speciality Hospital Ethics Committee, Bengaluru, India (registration ECR/1324/Inst/KA/2019/RR-24) on 19 September 2026.
Pilots are identified only by study code (P01-P13), and names, account identifiers, email addresses, staff numbers and device session identifiers were removed before analysis.

Each pilot wore an Ultrahuman smart ring (Ultrahuman Healthcare Pvt Ltd, Bangalore, India) during the monitoring period.
The ring carries a triaxial accelerometer, a photoplethysmography sensor and a skin-temperature sensor.
Each night it records sleep timing, total sleep time, movement and awakenings between sleep onset and final waking, sleep stages and peripheral temperature.
The primary outcome was total sleep time, the quantity on which the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society base their sleep-duration recommendation (Watson et al. 2015).

text.text: The secondary outcome was the Ultrahuman sleep score, which runs from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating better sleep quality.
Its inputs are sleep duration, efficiency, awakenings and the consistency of sleep timing.
It also draws on skin temperature, sleep staging and sleeping heart rate.
Because duration is one of its inputs, the score is not independent of total sleep time.
It adds aspects of sleep quality, such as efficiency and the share of time in restorative sleep, that duration alone does not capture.
We also report wake after sleep onset, sleep efficiency, and the deep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep shares.
Every pilot wore the same device model, and all data passed through the same processing.
We analyzed each pilot's main sleep sessions.
Naps were outside the scope of this analysis.
We excluded sessions longer than 15 h, a recording artifact, and sleep taken during a flight (Schedule linkage).

Five nights held two main-sleep sessions, and both were kept, so counts of nights below are counts of sessions.

Pilots received each month's roster, with its departure times, during the previous month.

text.text: In this observational study of 13 cargo pilots tracked over six months, we found that sleep duration was shorter within the 24 h before departure and after landing.
The night before a flight was 48 min shorter than the pilot's rest nights, and the first sleep after one 28 min shorter, while later nights matched rest nights.
The magnitude of these differences varied with local departure and landing times.
The night before a morning departure was about an hour shorter than before an evening departure.
The first sleep after a landing between midnight and 06:00h was about an hour and a half shorter than after an evening landing.
The direction and length of the flight showed no association.
Sleep before morning departures was shorter, without corresponding differences in sleep continuity: efficiency and wake after sleep onset did not differ.
We propose that these nights were truncated, ending early but keeping their continuity.
Deep, slow-wave sleep is concentrated early in the night (Borbély 1982), so an early end removes little of it.
text.formatted: Deep, slow-wave sleep is concentrated early in the night <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Borbély 1982)</ref>, so an early end removes little of it.

text.text: It then makes up a larger share of a shorter night, as observed.
Anticipatory arousal would be expected to fragment sleep, which we did not see, though these data cannot exclude it.
This difference matches passenger-pilot studies of early starts (Roach et al. 2012; Vejvoda et al. 2014) and extends it to cargo.

Variation between pilots exceeded the variation explained by duty-cycle position.

Pilots' mean sleep ranged from 5.8 to 8.2 h, a spread more than twice the loss on the night before a flight.

Sleep duration was shorter within 24 h before departure and after landing, with a larger reduction before departure.

Figure 4: Total sleep time by the clock time of the flight next to it, as each night's deviation from the pilot's rest-night baseline.
Panel (a): the night before a departure, by local departure time.
Panel (b): the first sleep after a landing, by local landing time.
Boxes show the median and interquartile range, and whiskers the 5th to 95th percentiles. 181 pre-flight nights and 277 post-flight nights, 13 pilots.
Figure 5: Total sleep time (a) and sleep score (b) on home and away nights, for the short-turn (six pilots) and extended-rotation (seven pilots) groups.
Location was recorded mainly on nights around a flight, so home nights are duty nights at base, not rest nights.
Bars show the group median of per-pilot means, and whiskers the interquartile range. 692 nights with a known sleep location.
Averaged over each trip away from base, our pilots slept 35 min less per night than on rest nights (Supplementary Results, Trip-level average).
Trips by short-turn pilots, mostly nights around a flight, averaged 61 min less, close to Gander's figure.

Trips by extended-rotation pilots averaged 14 min less, in line with their smaller loss away from base.The preceding flight's direction and haul class showed no significant association with sleep, within intervals of about an hour either way.
As aircrew on short layovers often do not readjust, direction may matter less than it does in travelers.
The null result is more likely a feature of this study than evidence of no effect.
In this network, direction and haul class largely coincided: westward sectors were almost all long-haul, north-south sectors almost all short-haul, and no north-south ultra-long-haul night occurred.
With 13 pilots, their effects could not be separated.
Larger studies across more varied route structures are needed to establish the effects of haul and direction.Deadhead sectors bring the same timezone shift without the duty.
Without them, the post-flight refit linked long-haul sectors to less sleep, a difference 13 pilots cannot attribute to the duty itself.
Departure delay was not associated with the subsequent sleep score.
Time off between flights may explain why short-turn pilots tended to sleep less away from base, while extended-rotation pilots tended to lose sleep score instead.
Short turns may leave too little time for a full night.
Longer layovers would let duration recover, while sleep out of phase with the body clock still scores lower.
If so, away-night sleep should lengthen with the layover before it.
After a night landing, a rest period planned as a block of hours may fall mostly in daylight.
Duty limits scale with the length of a duty, its start time and the time zones it crosses (European Aviation Safety Agency 2014; Federal Aviation Administration 2012).
In this network, sleep varied with the clock times of departure and landing but not with the length or direction of the flight.
Fatigue risk management could therefore plan rest around both departure and landing times, measured against each pilot's own sleep.
